title: Advanced Grammar (Essential Grammar in Use - Murphy)
lesson_overview: C1 level covers nuanced meanings, complex structures, and register awareness for sophisticated academic and professional communication.

topics.name: Nuanced Modals
topics.lesson_text: Modal verbs with fine distinctions in meaning. Might vs may: might = slightly less probable, more tentative. Must vs have to: must = personal conviction, strong deduction; have to = external obligation. Can't vs couldn't: can't = present ability impossibility; couldn't = past ability impossibility. Needn't vs don't have to: needn't = unnecessary (don't need to), don't have to = not required. Should have + past participle = criticism of past action: You should have told me. Could have + past participle = missed possibility. May have + past participle = deduction about past. Note: Modals often interchangeable with slight nuance differences; context determines best choice.
examples: You look tired. You might be working too hard.
He isn't here. He must have gone home.
You should have called me yesterday.

topics.name: Complex Structures
topics.lesson_text: Participle clauses (-ing/-ed) for concise information: The man waiting at the station is my father (active participle). The excited children running in the park (active). The bored students listening to the lecture (passive). Reduced relative clauses: The book (which) I bought is interesting. Non-defining relative clauses: extra information, commas: My brother, who lives in London, is a doctor. Defining vs non-defining: essential vs extra info. Participle clauses without subject change: Seeing is believing. Note: Participle clauses must have different subject from main clause.
examples: Opening the door, she went out.
The movie, directed by Spielberg, was excellent.
The audience fascinated by the performance gave a standing ovation.

topics.name: Register
topics.lesson_text: Register variation based on context, audience, purpose. Formal: passive structures, complex sentences, impersonal structures, sophisticated vocabulary (receive vs get, commence vs start). Informal: phrasal verbs, simple sentences, colloquial expressions, contractions. Literary: archaic vocabulary, inverted structures, complex syntax. Everyday: neutral, direct. Register markers: formal connectives (therefore, furthermore), informal linkers (so, anyway). Note: Same meaning can be expressed differently depending on register; academic writing requires formal register, casual conversation allows informal.
examples: Formal: I would be grateful if you could reply. Informal: Reply if you can.
Literary: 'Twas the night before Christmas. Everyday: It was Christmas Eve.

topics.name: Ellipsis & Substitution
topics.lesson_text: Ellipsis: omitting repeated words/clauses with same meaning. Nominal ellipsis: 'The red car is faster than the green (car).' Verbless clauses: 'Happy to help.' After 'so', 'such', 'as': 'He is so good a player (that) we all admire him.' Substitution one/ones: 'I prefer the red one.' do-support substitution: 'I like tea.' 'So do I.' Note: Ellipsis common in informal speech and writing; substitution avoids repetition. Must maintain clarity and not create ambiguity. Note: 'so...that' structure with ellipsis: 'It was such a good film (that) I saw it twice.'
examples: I like this shirt more than that (one).
She is a better singer than I (am).
Such was the success that everyone celebrated.

cefr_description: Can express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions.
